blocks.text: Mean Average Precision, MAP, extends the rank-aware thinking of MRR from the previous lesson to every relevant item in a ranked list, not just the first one, for each query it computes Average Precision, the mean of the precision values measured at each position where a relevant item appears, then averages that across every test query, producing a single score that rewards a system for placing all of its relevant results as early as possible, not merely the first.

1. The Gap MAP Fills

MRR, from the previous lesson, only rewards how quickly the first relevant item appears and ignores everything after it, but many real retrieval tasks genuinely care about surfacing every relevant item as early as possible, not just the first, MAP is built specifically to reward exactly that, giving credit for every relevant item found, weighted by how early it appears.

blocks.title: A useful framing
blocks.content: MRR asks how fast is the first win, MAP asks how good is the whole ranking at surfacing every win early, both are rank-aware, but MAP considers strictly more information per query.

blocks.text: This makes MAP a natural default whenever a task sits between the two extremes, more than one correct answer exists, but their exact positions within the ranking still matter a great deal to the user experience.
2. Precision at Each Relevant Position

The building block of Average Precision is precision computed at the exact position of every relevant item in the ranked list, if the second relevant item appears at rank 5, precision is computed using only the first 5 results, counting how many of those 5 are relevant, this gives one precision value for every relevant item found, rather than a single precision value for the whole list.

Notice that precision values computed this way are non-increasing at first glance, but can actually fluctuate depending on how many irrelevant items sit between consecutive relevant ones, a long run of irrelevant items between two relevant ones lowers precision noticeably at the second relevant position.

blocks.title: A quick sanity check
blocks.content: The final precision value in this list, computed at the position of the very last relevant item found, always equals the total relevant items found divided by the length of the ranking up to that point.

blocks.text: 3. Average Precision for a Single Query

Average Precision is the mean of those precision-at-relevant-position values, computed for a single query, if no relevant items are found at all, Average Precision is defined as 0, this single number summarizes, for one query, how consistently relevant items were placed early throughout the ranking.

code.content:
def average_precision(ranked_results, relevant_set):
    precisions = precisions_at_relevant_positions(ranked_results, relevant_set)
    return sum(precisions) / len(relevant_set) if relevant_set else 0.0

print(average_precision(results, relevant))   # (1.0 + 0.667 + 0.6) / 3 = 0.756

# a ranking with relevant items clustered near the top scores higher
print(average_precision(['a','b','c','d'], {'a','b'}))   # relevant at 1 and 2
print(average_precision(['x','a','y','b'], {'a','b'}))   # relevant at 2 and 4, lower score

# an empty relevant set is a defined edge case, not an error
print(average_precision([a,b,c], set()))   # 0.0 by convention

blocks.text: 4. Why Divide by the Total Relevant Count, Not Hits Found

Average Precision divides the sum of precision values by the total number of relevant items that exist for the query, not just the number actually found, this means missing a relevant item entirely still lowers the score, exactly like Recall@K, this design choice makes Average Precision sensitive to both ranking quality and completeness at the same time.

This is exactly the same denominator convention used by Recall@K, dividing by the true, complete count of relevant items rather than only the ones actually observed, which is why Average Precision is sometimes described as combining recall-style completeness with precision-style ranking quality in a single number.

A system that returns only its most confident relevant item and stops there, ignoring several other genuinely relevant items entirely, still receives a penalty under this convention, since those missed items reduce the shared denominator relative to the small sum of precision values actually achieved.
5. Mean Average Precision Across Queries

MAP averages Average Precision across a whole set of test queries, just as MRR averages reciprocal rank, giving a single overall score that summarizes how well the system tends to rank all relevant items early, across the full range of queries it needs to handle.

MAP, much like MRR, is typically reported as a single overall number for a whole benchmark or test set, making it easy to track over time as a retrieval or ranking system is improved, and to compare directly against other candidate systems evaluated on the same test queries.

Because MAP folds together both ranking order and completeness into a single number, teams sometimes also report the underlying Precision@K and Recall@K curves alongside it, to diagnose exactly which aspect is driving a MAP change.
6. MAP vs MRR

MRR only looks at the position of the first relevant item, MAP considers the position of every relevant item, if a system consistently finds the first relevant item quickly but buries the rest deep in the ranking, MRR would score it well while MAP would correctly penalize it for the poorly placed remaining relevant items.

blocks.text: Choosing between MRR and MAP ultimately comes down to how the retrieved results will actually be consumed, a single best answer scenario favors MRR, a full list of results a user is expected to browse favors MAP.
7. MAP vs Recall@K and Precision@K

Precision@K and Recall@K are both computed at one fixed cutoff K, MAP instead effectively considers every possible cutoff at once, by evaluating precision at each position where a relevant item actually appears, this makes MAP a single number that already summarizes performance across the whole ranking, rather than requiring a separate score at every candidate K.

This all-cutoffs-at-once property is a major reason MAP became the standard summary metric in classic information retrieval evaluation, avoiding the need to separately report Precision@K and Recall@K at many different values of K.

blocks.text: 8. MAP in Document Retrieval

MAP has long been the standard metric in classic information retrieval benchmarks, where a query typically has several genuinely relevant documents scattered throughout a large collection, and a good system needs to surface all of them reasonably early, not just the very first one.

Early web search evaluation competitions relied heavily on MAP specifically because a search result page for an informational query often has many genuinely relevant documents scattered throughout a large collection, not just one single correct answer.
9. MAP at a Bounded Cutoff: MAP@K

Just like MRR can be bounded to MRR@K, MAP can also be computed only within a fixed top K, this MAP@K variant only considers relevant items that appear within the first K positions when computing Average Precision, matching the same fixed-window evaluation used by Precision@K and Recall@K.

code.content:
def average_precision_at_k(ranked_results, relevant_set, k):
    top_k = ranked_results[:k]
    precisions = precisions_at_relevant_positions(top_k, relevant_set)
    return sum(precisions) / len(relevant_set) if relevant_set else 0.0

blocks.text: MAP@K is particularly useful whenever evaluating the full, unbounded ranking is impractical or unrealistic, such as when a user interface only ever displays a fixed number of results per page.
10. Why MAP Rewards Clustering Relevant Items Early

Because Average Precision sums a precision value computed at every relevant position, and precision itself is highest when fewer irrelevant items have been seen so far, a ranking that clusters all its relevant items near the top scores much higher under MAP than one that spreads the same relevant items evenly throughout a long list, even if both rankings find exactly the same total number of relevant items.

This clustering reward is exactly why a system that reorders its top results to move known-relevant items earlier, without changing which items are included at all, will see its MAP score improve even though its Recall@K stays exactly the same.
11. MAP in Recommendation Systems

A recommendation system generating a ranked list of suggested items for a user is commonly evaluated with MAP, since a good recommender is expected to surface multiple items the user will actually engage with, not just get lucky with a single top pick, exactly the multi-item, rank-sensitive reward MAP is built to measure.

code.content:
# MAP applied to a ranked list of recommended items for one user
recommended = ['movie1','movie2','movie3','movie4']
watched = {'movie2','movie4'}
print(average_precision(recommended, watched))

blocks.text: 12. Interpolated Average Precision

Some classic information retrieval formulations use a variant called interpolated Average Precision, which smooths out the precision values by taking, at each recall level, the maximum precision achieved at that level or any later point in the ranking, this variant produces a slightly more optimistic but smoother precision-recall curve, though the basic, uninterpolated version described earlier in this lesson remains more common in modern machine learning evaluation.

The interpolated variant traces back to early information retrieval research where precision-recall curves were often plotted at a small set of standard recall levels, smoothing local dips in precision that would otherwise make the curve look artificially jagged.

Modern machine learning papers and libraries, including most standard implementations found in popular evaluation toolkits, typically use the plain, uninterpolated Average Precision described earlier in this lesson rather than the older interpolated variant.
13. The Relationship Between MAP and the Precision-Recall Curve

Average Precision for a single query is mathematically equivalent to the area under that query precision-recall curve, a concept related to the ROC and precision-recall curves covered generally elsewhere in this curriculum, MAP can be understood as averaging this area-under-the-curve quantity across every test query.

This area-under-the-curve interpretation is a useful mental shortcut, a ranking with a high Average Precision has, roughly speaking, a precision-recall curve that stays high across a wide range of recall values, rather than dropping off sharply.

This connection to area under the precision-recall curve is also why MAP is sometimes referred to informally as an approximation to the area under that curve, computed at the specific set of recall levels where a relevant item actually appears.
14. A Worked Example
Compute Average Precision for a query with 5 ranked results where 3 items are relevant, appearing at positions 1, 3, and 5.

code.content:
results = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
relevant = {"a", "c", "e"}
precisions = precisions_at_relevant_positions(results, relevant)
print(precisions)                     # [1.0, 0.667, 0.6]
print(sum(precisions) / len(relevant))   # 0.756

blocks.title: Interpreting the result
blocks.content: An Average Precision of 0.756 here reflects that the three relevant items were found reasonably early, at positions 1, 3, and 5, rather than being pushed toward the end of a much longer ranked list.

blocks.text: Comparing this same worked example against a version where the relevant items instead appeared at positions 3, 4, and 5 would show a noticeably lower Average Precision, directly illustrating the clustering reward discussed earlier.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing Average Precision, a per-query score, with Mean Average Precision, MAP, the average of Average Precision across many queries.
Dividing the sum of precision values by the number of relevant items found instead of the true total number of relevant items, silently inflating the score when items are missed.
Using MAP for a task where only one correct answer genuinely matters, where MRR would give a clearer, more directly interpretable signal.
Forgetting that MAP, unlike Precision@K or Recall@K, has no explicit cutoff K, it considers the full ranked list unless a bounded variant is deliberately defined.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is comparing MAP scores computed with different total counts of relevant items per query as if they measured exactly the same thing, MAP already normalizes per query, but the underlying difficulty of each query can still vary a great deal.

A fifth common mistake is applying MAP to a task with only ever one possible relevant answer per query, where it collapses down to being numerically identical to reciprocal rank, making MRR the simpler, equally accurate choice.
16. Practice: Compute MAP for Your Own Query Set

Build 3 small ranked lists with known relevant items scattered at different positions, compute Average Precision for each, then compute the overall MAP and confirm it matches the average of the 3 individual Average Precision values.

A useful extension of this practice exercise is deliberately reordering one of the ranked lists to push its relevant items later, confirming that Average Precision for that query drops as a direct result.

A further worthwhile extension is comparing MAP@5 against the full, unbounded MAP for the same query set, observing how much of the overall score is determined just by the earliest handful of results.
Key Takeaway

MAP extends the rank-aware idea behind MRR to every relevant item in the ranking, not just the first, by averaging precision at each position a relevant item appears, then averaging that across every test query, rewarding systems that place all of their relevant results early, not merely one.

This lesson builds directly on MRR from the previous lesson and Precision@K and Recall@K from earlier ones, and connects forward to NDCG, which extends this same rank-aware philosophy even further to handle graded, non-binary relevance judgments.

The clustering-reward property covered in the newly added section is precisely why MAP is often preferred over Recall@K alone whenever the exact position of relevant items within the ranking, not just whether they appear at all, genuinely matters to the end user.
